metadata.title: The Cell Next Door
metadata.subtitle: the same mistake, three sizes
metadata.presenter: Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI
metadata.builder_note: multi-act, ~9 min. Structure is CONCENTRIC: one misreading at three scales, each closer to the narrator. See STRUCTURE-DIFF.md.
metadata.duration_note: Both figures are planning numbers. Measured Kokoro audio overwrites estimated_duration_s and becomes the master clock; never hand-repair timing.

props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI · The Cell Next Door

beats.narration_text: Here's a sentence from a science video about cancer immunotherapy. "Pembrolizumab produces five-year survival above fifty percent in metastatic melanoma." It's a good sentence. Specific — it names the drug, it names the disease, it has a number in it. Sounds like someone checked. Someone did check. The same project ran a fact-check on that sentence, caught it, and wrote down a correction: not fifty percent — about forty-three. The real number is thirty-eight point seven percent. So the claim was wrong. And the correction was also wrong. Both of them are sitting in the same table, in the same paper, one cell away from the truth.

legibility.artifact: The narrated sentence in full-width type, held. Then the fact-check's own correction line as a second card beneath it. Then a third: 38.7%, with "Robert et al., Lancet Oncology 2019;20(9):1239–1251" legible underneath. Each held 3 s at the moment of assertion.

beats.narration_text: Hi — this is Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI. That mistake is the subject of this video, and the reason is that it doesn't stay that size. It's also, as it happens, the reason cancer immunotherapy works spectacularly in some tumours and not at all in others. Let's start with the table.

legibility.artifact: Title card, plain-language subject line, presenter credit. Held 2 s.

notes.structural_note: This beat deliberately withholds the shape — no framework, no "three things," no promise of a turn. "It doesn't stay that size" is the only signal, and it is meant to read as a figure of speech on first listen. See STRUCTURE-DIFF.md.

beats.narration_text: KEYNOTE oh-oh-six. Eight hundred and thirty-four patients with advanced melanoma, randomised to pembrolizumab or ipilimumab. Five-year survival, everyone in the trial: thirty-eight point seven percent. So "above fifty" isn't this row. The fact-check's forty-three is real — forty-three point two percent — but it belongs to the subgroup who'd had no previous treatment. Not everyone. One column across. And now the thing that makes this trial almost unfair. Thirty-eight point seven percent alive at five years, for everybody. Thirty-eight point seven months of median survival, for first-liners. Same digits. One is a proportion, the other is a length of time, and they sit a few lines apart on the same page. Nobody made anything up. People read a table, and this table has cells that look like each other.

legibility.artifact: A four-cell grid built live — rows all patients / first line, columns 5-year OS / median OS. Cells fill as spoken: 38.7% · 43.2% · 32.7 mo · 38.7 mo. The two 38.7s light simultaneously and stay lit for the rest of the beat, one tagged percent, the other tagged months, in type large enough to read the unit. Units are the whole visual argument — if a viewer can read the digits but not the unit, the frame has failed. Citation persistent in the lower third throughout.

beats.narration_text: Here's what should bother you. In the same trial, the comparison arm — ipilimumab, the previous standard of care — had a median overall survival of fifteen point nine months. And they kept following these patients. The ten-year results came out in twenty twenty-four. Thirty-four percent of the pembrolizumab group were still alive. A decade later. Against twenty-three point six percent on ipilimumab. That is an extraordinary result. One of the genuinely great results in modern oncology. The overclaim bought nothing — there was nothing wrong with the truth.

legibility.artifact: Both survival curves, ipilimumab median marked at 15.9 months, the 5-year point marked at 38.7%. Then the timeline extends and the 10-year point lands at 34.0%, with "Long et al., Annals of Oncology 2024;35(12):1191–1199" legible beneath it. Held 4 s.

notes.note: Do not use the source reel's "historical median of nine months." No citation exists anywhere in the source, and the real benchmark could not be pinned to a primary text this pass (RESEARCH.md Part 5, item 1). The in-trial comparator is verified; use only that.

beats.act: THE SAME MOVE, ONE SIZE UP
beats.tone: brisk; the pattern starting to show
beats.narration_text: Now watch the same move happen to a statistic the whole field quotes. There's a famous one-page letter in the New England Journal — Yarchoan and colleagues, twenty seventeen — that plots response rate against mutation count across twenty-seven cancer types. The correlation is zero point seven four. And that letter is cited, constantly, as mutation count predicts who responds. Zero point seven four squared is zero point five five. Mutation count explains fifty-five percent of the difference between cancer types — which means it does not explain forty-five percent. Same table, cell next door.

legibility.artifact: The regression curve alone, on a log TMB axis, with r = 0.74 · r² = 0.55 · 27 tumour types as the kicker. No anchors, no residuals yet — the line as the field quotes it. Held 3 s at "cell next door".

notes.structural_note: split out of the old 53-second B05, which carried seven claims and did three jobs at once. This beat states the statistic; B05B measures it.

beats.narration_text: So we went and checked where that forty-five percent lives. Their own formula predicts pancreatic cancer's failure to within half a percentage point. It handles mismatch-repair-deficient colorectal well. Where it breaks is microsatellite-stable colorectal — the formula says about nine percent should respond, and in the trial, zero of eighteen patients did. Not low. None.

legibility.artifact: The same curve returns unchanged and the three anchors drop onto it as numbered residual bars, keyed to a legend strip below the axis — ① pancreatic (−0.6), ② MSS colorectal (−8.9 · 0 of 18), ③ dMMR colorectal (−3.4). The MSS bar is the largest object in the plot and is held 4 s. Same grammar as B12: nothing removed, only added. Inline labels were tried first and abandoned twice: they crossed the regression line, and a legend placed inside the plot with an opaque fill occluded the curve between TMB 3 and 20 — hiding data is worse than a label sitting on it. The legend lives outside the axes where it cannot collide with anything.

notes.receipt: every number here is reproduced by experiment/tmb_orr_audit.py.

beats.tone: quieter; the cleanest evidence in the act
beats.narration_text: And the cleanest one is inside a single cancer. In Merkel-cell carcinoma, the tumours driven by a virus carry far fewer mutations than the ones driven by sun damage. The low-mutation ones responded better. Sixteen patients and nine, so that's an illustration and not a result — but it points the right way.

legibility.artifact: Two labelled groups side by side, nothing else on the slate — 62% in accent against virus-positive · low mutation burden · 10 of 16, and 44% against virus-negative · UV-driven, high burden · 4 of 9. Beneath them, one line: the lower-burden group responded better. Then "n = 16 / n = 9 — illustration, not result" burned in and persistent for the rest of the beat. Split out of B05B, which was carrying the regression residuals and this counterexample on one frame. They are two different kinds of evidence — a model's error, and a case that contradicts the model's variable — and this one is the strongest single piece in the act. It earns its own slate and the room to be read.

beats.act: AND AGAIN, IN A TRIAL'S OWN REPORT
beats.narration_text: Once more, bigger. A randomised trial: high-dose radiation to one tumour site, then immunotherapy — the idea being that the wreckage acts like a vaccine and warms the tumour up. Seventy-six patients with lung cancer. Response rate went from eighteen percent to thirty-six. A doubling. That is how it gets described. The trial set two bars in advance. It needed a response rate of fifty percent, at a p-value under zero point one. It came in at thirty-six percent, with a p-value of zero point zero seven. So it cleared the statistical bar and missed the response bar. The paper's own conclusion: the criteria for clinical benefit were not met. And "a doubling" is the cell next door to that. Though I'll come back to this one, because it has a complication I don't get to skip.

legibility.artifact: Both prespecified thresholds drawn first — the 50% ORR line and the p<0.10 condition — as a two-part target card. Then the observed values land against them: 36% sits visibly below the ORR line while p=0.07 sits inside the p condition, each marked pass/fail independently. Held 5 s. The frame must not let a viewer read p=0.07 as the failure.

beats.narration_text: So far, every mistake has been arithmetic — a number read next to the right number. Now the interesting one, which isn't about numbers at all. Immunotherapy doesn't attack cancer. It takes a brake off a T cell that's already attacking — the last of those six links. Every one before it has to have happened first. And that's where hot, cold, and excluded come from. A hot tumour has T cells inside it. A cold one has none anywhere near it. An excluded one has T cells at the edge, stuck outside, unable to get in. Release the brake on a T cell that isn't there and you've released a brake on nothing.

legibility.artifact: The six-link chain assembles left to right, each link labelled in plain words as spoken and persisting. Then three tumour cross-sections beneath it — hot, cold, excluded — T cells drawn in the position each label describes. Chain stays up for the rest of the act.

notes.structural_note: vocabulary, not an instrument panel. The viewer is never asked to apply this. It is the thing the next two trials disagree about.

beats.tone: even; let the finding do the work
beats.narration_text: If a cold tumour has no immune response, start one. There's a pathway called STING that does exactly that when it detects DNA where DNA shouldn't be. So: inject a drug that switches it on, straight into the tumour. Phase one. Forty-seven patients. One confirmed partial response. But read what they measured. They took biopsies before and after. Immune cell infiltration into the tumour: no significant change. Meanwhile, in the bloodstream — exactly what they'd hoped for. Inflammatory signalling up. T cell populations expanding. The drug worked. The pathway switched on. The immune system woke up, and it never showed up at the tumour. One footnote. The single patient who did respond had Merkel-cell carcinoma — the virus-driven cancer from earlier. The one tumour in that trial that was never cold to begin with.

legibility.artifact: Split panel, both halves legible simultaneously and held 5 s at "it never showed up at the tumour." Left: paired before/after biopsy infiltration, flat, labelled no significant change. Right: peripheral cytokines and T-cell clonal expansion, rising. Citation persistent.

notes.precision_note: the trial reported one confirmed PR plus two unconfirmed (parotid, myxofibrosarcoma), and lesion size was stable or decreased in 94% of evaluable injected lesions. The narration says "one confirmed partial response," which is correct. Any on-screen response count must read 1 confirmed / 2 unconfirmed — the visual must not assert something narrower than the paper.

beats.narration_text: Different target. Pancreatic cancer is the textbook excluded tumour: T cells reach the edge and stop, held off by dense surrounding tissue and a chemical signal called CXCL12. Block the receptor that reads it, and the door should open. In mice, it did. In people: thirty-seven patients enrolled, twenty-nine evaluable, the CXCR4 blocker plus pembrolizumab, no chemotherapy. CD8 effector T cells inside the tumour: increased. Suppressive myeloid cells: decreased. Regulatory T cells in circulation: decreased. Every single thing the hypothesis predicted — confirmed, in human tissue. Response rate: three point four percent. One patient. The door opened. The T cells walked in. Nothing happened.

legibility.artifact: Three measured immunologic endpoints as before/after bars, all moving the predicted direction, each labelled. Then the clinical endpoint drops in beside them at 3.4%, at the same scale, held 5 s. The contrast between three moved bars and one flat outcome is the beat — do not cut away.

beats.narration_text: Put those two side by side. They don't agree. The first drug: the immune system activated, and the T cells never arrived. The second: the T cells arrived, and nothing died. Opposite findings. And the same chart. Roughly nothing, both times. Which means "it didn't work" was never the useful sentence. Two questions were. Which link did this actually target — and did the next link move? First drug: targeted priming. Priming moved. Trafficking didn't. It broke at link four. Second drug: targeted trafficking. Trafficking moved, measured in tissue. Killing didn't. It broke at link six. Two drugs, two completely different broken links, one identical result. So "cold tumour" isn't a diagnosis — it's a symptom. And the same symptom has at least two causes, which is exactly why a fix for one does nothing for the other.

legibility.artifact: The chain from B07 returns. STING lights link three, breaks visibly at four. CXCR4 lights four through five, breaks at six. Both paths terminate at the same flat outcome marker. The two questions appear only now, as persistent text, and stay for the rest of the film.

notes.structural_note: this is the first appearance of the framework, ~70% into the film. It is derived from the contradiction in B08/B09; neither beat alone produces it. Do not foreshadow it earlier.

beats.narration_text: Right. Now run that on me. Twice in this video I told you mutation count leaves forty-five percent unexplained. That's one minus zero point seven four squared, and it's the number sitting right there next to the correlation. But a lot of those response rates come from ten or twenty patients, and small samples make any correlation look weaker than it really is. We modelled that. Correcting for it, the honest figure is closer to forty percent. Forty-five was the cell next door. I used it twice, in a video about not doing that, and I'd have kept it if we hadn't run the model.

legibility.artifact: The attenuation curve from tmb_orr_audit.py with 45% and 40% both marked, [ILLUSTRATIVE MODEL] burned in for the full beat. Held 4 s. The B05 frame briefly returns beneath it with "45%" struck through.

beats.narration_text: And a worse one, because this time I chose it. That radiation trial. I told you it missed the bar it set for itself, which is true. What I didn't tell you is the rest of the paper. The patients who benefited most were the ones whose tumours were PD-L1-negative — the colder ones. Which is a point for the whole warming-up idea, inside a trial that formally failed. I had a tidy argument running and I handed you the half of that trial that fitted it. Same move as reaching for "above fifty" when the answer is thirty-eight point seven percent. Pick the cell that suits you.

legibility.artifact: The B06 frame returns intact — 50% bar, 18%, 36% — and the PD-L1-negative subgroup result drops in beside it, clearly marked subgroup. Both held together for 4 s; neither is removed from frame. The visual promise is that nothing was taken away, only added back.

notes.structural_note: this pays the promise made at the end of B06. Do not build the beat sheet with B06's closing clause and this beat out of sync — they are one unit.

beats.narration_text: And then the one underneath all of them. I've been saying "pancreatic cancer is an excluded tumour" — as though that's a fact about pancreatic cancer. It isn't. Profile the immune cells patient by patient and pancreatic tumours split into at least two distinct types. Which one a patient has predicts how long they live. So hot, cold, and excluded aren't categories of cancer. They're descriptions of a sample. Ask "is pancreatic cancer cold?" and you've asked the wrong shape of question — and I asked it, out loud, for most of this video. So there's the ladder. A number read one cell over. A field reporting the mechanism it moved instead of the outcome it missed. Me handing you the half of a trial that suited my argument. And underneath all of it, a category error I couldn't see because I was standing inside it.

legibility.artifact: The two PDAC immune profiles side by side with their divergent survival, citation legible, held 4 s. Then, briefly, the four instances stacked as one column — the table cell, the two trials, B12, this beat — the only moment the film's own shape is shown.

beats.narration_text: So, the thing to do with it. Pick any immunotherapy readout — press release, abstract, conference slide, doesn't matter. Run the two questions. Which link did this target? Did that link move — is there a measurement, in human tissue, not a mouse? And did the next link move? You pass if you can name the link and point at the measurement. You fail if the report hands you the clinical endpoint or the mechanism and never both. That failure is extremely common, and now you can see it. The script that produced every number in this video is in the description. Two seconds to run, nothing to install.

legibility.artifact: The two questions filled in as a worked example on a real readout — link named, measurement named, pass/fail marked. Not a blank template. Repo path and run command legible for 4 s.

beats.narration_text: The Cell Next Door. Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI — signing off.

legibility.artifact: Title, then Tanmay Kulkarni · @HumanitariansAI — the presenter credit, not the brand twice. No URL. Beneath it, "sources in the description · every number reproducible", which the outro no longer says aloud because B14 already handed over the script and the run command; a spoken line after "signing off" undercuts the sign-off.
